title: The first gray hair
hookLine: King Makhadeva tells his barber to report the first gray hair, and then goes forth

lines: ONE GRAY HAIR IN THE MIRROR.
cards: The bathroom mirror, a Tuesday morning, and there it is: one gray hair, wiry, catching the light. It can be plucked, dyed, or laughed off. Or it can be read as news.
The Buddha is walking through a mango grove near the city of Mithilā, and at one spot he smiles. Ānanda knows the Buddha doesn't smile without a reason, and asks why.
The Buddha tells him a story about a king who once lived on this very ground, his barber, and a pair of tweezers.

teach.h: TELL ME WHEN YOU SEE GRAY.
teach.b: Long ago, the story goes, a good king named Makhādeva ruled here. He gave his barber an unusual order: whenever you see gray hairs growing on my head, tell me. Years pass, many years in the story's long, legendary count.
One day the barber sees one. He plucks it out with tweezers and lays it in the king's palm.
The king looks at it and says the gray hairs are messengers of the gods, and they've arrived. It's time.
He gives the barber a whole village as thanks, calls his eldest son, and hands him the kingdom with one request: when you see your first gray hair, do the same.

teach.h: PASS IT ON, AND GO FORTH.
teach.b: Pass the kingdom on, and go forth. Then he shaves his head, puts on robes, and lives the rest of his life in this same mango grove, filling the world around him with kindness and compassion.
His son keeps the promise, and his son's son, for a long line of kings. Until one king doesn't, and the good custom ends with him. Then the Buddha reveals two things.
First, I was King Makhādeva. Second, that old practice was good, but it led only to a heavenly world. What I teach now, he says, leads all the way to peace and awakening.
And he gives Ānanda the same charge the old king gave his son: keep this good practice going.
In this story the gray hair isn't a tragedy. It's a messenger, and its message isn't, you're old. It's, the time you were waiting for has come.

how: Buddhists in several countries take temporary or late-life ordination, and older lay people often deepen their practice, keeping extra precepts and spending more time at the temple, as a way of answering the 'messengers' of age.

o: a messenger of the gods, like a first gray hair
the royal barber who watches the king's hair
a heavenly being who guards a royal line

s: the Buddha smiled at the spot where the story happened
Ānanda asked why, and the Buddha told the story of Makhādeva.
the king had the barber punished for finding gray hair
he gave the barber a whole village as thanks.
the Buddha says the old king's practice led all the way to awakening
he says it led to a heavenly world; his own teaching leads further.

games.q: you're King Makhādeva. your barber has just laid a gray hair in your palm. what do you do?
o: hand the kingdom to your son and go forth
games.why: he calls the gray hairs messengers of the gods, gives the barber a village, passes the kingdom on and goes forth.

practice: Ask yourself what your messenger is. It may not be a hair: a slower knee, a child who no longer needs you, a friend's diagnosis, a birthday with a zero.
Let one come to mind, and instead of flinching, ask what it might be inviting you to begin, or to pass on.

wordCard.voice: Devaduta. King Makhādeva's barber laid it in his palm, and the king called it a messenger and went forth.

orig.note: Pali devadūta: messenger of the gods. the name the king gives his gray hairs.

carryVoice: Your line: the time has come. A sign of time can be read as news. Week sixty-seven, done: the fire, views, the leper's fire, tested teachings, Raṭṭhapāla's fast, four summaries, and the first gray hair.
